body_markdown:
Volkswagen canceled it at the last minute, and purists still scoff at it today. And yet, the Porsche 924 played a significant role in the company’s history by charting a new course, and it sold nearly as well as the emblematic 911 during its 12-year production run. We borrowed a 1980 example from the Porsche museum to find out why it deserves more respect as it celebrates its 50th anniversary.


The 924 project started in March 1972, when Volkswagen asked Porsche to develop a replacement for[the 914](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/2020-hagerty-bull-market-selection-1970-76-porsche-914/) . While the 914 was a Porsche project that was sold jointly with Volkswagen, the new car (which was called EA 425 internally) was envisioned solely as a Volkswagen. This largely explains why it featured a front-mounted, water-cooled straight-four engine, which was a layout that Porsche had never put into production. The project reached the pre-production stage, but Volkswagen canceled it in late 1974. The reasons behind this decision remain vague, even over five decades later. Odds are that several factors played a role, including the 1973 oil crisis, concerns that the 924 would overlap with[the Scirocco](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1981-volkswagen-scirocco-karmann-ghia-ii/) , and Volkswagen’s shift toward[more mainstream models](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/your-handy-1974-84-volkswagen-golf-rabbit-mk1-buyers-guide/) .


Porsche was still interested, though; it needed an entry-level car. It purchased the EA 425 project from Volkswagen, made several updates inside and out (including redesigning the cylinder head), and launched it as the 924 in 1976. Audi built the car in Neckarsulm, Germany, which earned the 924 the reputation as the black sheep of the Porsche family. It’s true, many of the parts that make up the 924 carry a Volkswagen parts number—you can’t unscramble this egg. But saying that it’s not a real Porsche is cruelly unfair.


The sketches and prototypes pictured below illustrate how the EA 425 changed as it transitioned into the 924. It’s clear that, early on, the goal was to start with a blank slate; the idea wasn’t to build an updated 914. The pop-up headlights, the wrap-around rear window, and the wedge-shaped silhouette were already dialed in. The front end changed surprisingly little as the car made the leap from the drawing board to the production line, but designers made the overall styling sharper and gave the rear end a new look.

“For us, the design and proportions were so cohesive that we were able to continue working without making any changes to the concept. That would have been impossible at such a late stage of development anyway,” explained designer Harm Lagaaij, who was on the team that worked on the car. He added that it helped that Porsche’s design language wasn’t as set in stone as it is today. The 911 was more of an aging flagship than an icon, so the 924’s forward-thinking proportions didn’t set off a five-alarm panic.


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


Sales in the United States started for the 1977 model year with a base price of $9,395, or about $52,300 in 2026. For context, that same year a 911 S started at $14,995 (about $83,400 today) and a Volkswagen Scirocco cost $5,295 (about $29,500 today). The 924[went through numerous evolutions](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/your-handy-1977-88-porsche-924-buyers-guide/) during the production run: Porsche quickly made a five-speed manual available, it released the 924 Turbo for 1980, and it launched many homologation specials (like the Carrera GT) and racing variants during the 1980s.


The[944](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/your-handy-1982-91-porsche-944-buyers-guide/) , introduced for 1983, was an offshoot of the 924 with a Porsche-designed 2.5-liter four-cylinder.[The V-8-powered 928](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/the-1978-95-porsche-928-no-longer-black-sheep/) , released in 1978, and[the 968](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/1992-95-porsche-968-getting-some-love/) that replaced the 944 in 1992 shared their basic transaxle layout with the 924. In short, this often-overlooked coupe had a lasting impact on the Porsche range. Production ended in 1988, and a total of 150,684 units were built (including the 924 S), according to Porsche’s archives department. It sold almost as well as the 911 over the same period.


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


The 1980 model we’re driving comes straight from the Porsche museum via[a stint in Hollywood](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/even-better-than-the-house-of-gucci-the-garage-of-gucci/) , and it has the psychedelic Pasha interior that was available in some markets. This isn’t a big car; it stretches about 166 inches long, 66 inches wide, and 50 inches tall, but our first impression after slipping behind the wheel is that it’s more spacious than its dimensions suggest. The layout is well thought-out, too: Everything is where you expect it to be, from the shifter to the window cranks. There’s only one door mirror, and some of the plastics feel cheap even by old-car standards, but the view over the long, sloping hood signals that this is a special car. It was an entry-level Porsche, sure, but it was still a Porsche, and it was out of reach for the average motorist when it was new.


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


Mechanically, the 924 feels almost as solid as an old-school Mercedes-Benz. It helps that Porsche owns and maintains the example that we’re driving, and its mileage is so low that we feel guilty every time the odometer moves. It gives us a perfect idea of what a well-sorted 924 should feel like, however: quick, confidence-inspiring, and a lot more fun to drive than many give it credit for.


The 125-horsepower, 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine in our European-market test car settles into a nice, even idle with a pleasant exhaust note, and it revs quickly when it’s time to move. If you’ve spent time behind the wheel of a classic Porsche, the 924 will feel like an old friend in the sense that the engine doesn’t reveal its true character until you’re well into the upper echelons of the rev range. Shift at 3,000 rpm, and you’ll miss the essence of the car; shift at 4,000 rpm or higher, and you’ll get it immediately.


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


Acceleration is strong and linear (Porsche quotes a 10.5-second sprint from zero to 62 mph, which was quick enough for the era), and the clutch is heavy but not to the point where your left leg feels like it ran a half-marathon after 10 minutes of city driving. The shifter is a little notchy in a charming, analog way because the linkage runs all the way to the rear axle. Thanks to the thin A-pillars and the wrap-around rear window, visibility is superb all the way around. It also feels right at home (and completely stable!) holding a steady 90 mph on the smooth German autobahn. It turns heads, too. We expected to fly under the radar, but we were surprised at the number of drivers who took pictures, smiled, and gave us a thumbs up. In its home country, the 924 isn’t written off as a strange outgrowth of Porsche’s bold 1970s expansion plans. It’s cool, respected, and admired.


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


The 924’s best quality isn’t the rev-happy engine. It’s the handling. The transaxle gives it the kind of balanced, buttoned-down composure that’s difficult to find in a classic. With a 48/52 weight distribution, it’s a world away from the tail-heavy 911. In many ways it reminds us of the Alfa Romeo Alfetta GT and[its derivatives](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/market-spotlight/your-handy-1981-87-alfa-romeo-gtv-6-buyers-guide/) , which isn’t surprising: The Italians used a transaxle as well. In most cars, you slow down before taking a curve. In the 924, you can keep your foot steady (or, if you’re confident, accelerate) and keep going like you’re on a slot-car track. Replicating this in 2026 wouldn’t be hard, but it would require a great deal of electronic wizardry. There’s none of it in the 924; it’s all in the chassis. That means it can bite if you push it too hard. You need to learn how to master the 924 before you can drive it the way Porsche intended, but it’s more forgiving than a 911 from the same era.


[Ronan Glon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rglon/)


Porsche developed the 924 as a road car, not a racer, so the suspension is tuned for compliance. And yet, it doesn’t lean into a turn like a Cessna; we didn’t notice a lot of body roll. The steering is quick and direct, giving you an accurate idea of what the front wheels are doing. When it comes time to stop, the brakes are strong enough to handle the power-to-weight ratio. The 125-horsepower output isn’t all that impressive by 2026 standards, but keep in mind the 924 weighs under 2,400 pounds. That’s about as light as[a current-gen Miata](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2024-mazda-miata-club-review-nd3s-the-charm/) .


So, is the 924 a real Porsche? Certainly, but let’s keep that between us so prices stay relatively affordable. Pricing for an early car normally[ranges](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/924/1978/1978-porsche-924) from about $7,000 to $13,000, while the later, more powerful 924 S[typically commands a premium](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/924/1988/1988-porsche-924-s) . Finding a good example may be your biggest challenge, as many were driven into the ground or turned into race cars years ago. Source a Porsche 924 that’s been babied for all of its life, and you’ll bag a fun, head-turning coupe that makes a great summer daily driver.
